paragraphs: Ugandan police are investigating the killing of a man whose headless body was found in Luwala, a village near Kampala, according to Al Jazeera. Police spokesperson Kituuma Rusoke told reporters on Monday that the victim was a male adult of around 50 and that the head had not yet been recovered. Relatives identified the body as Robert Kabera, and police said the killing likely took place late on October 16 or early on October 17.

Kabera was a former sergeant who fled Rwanda several years ago and was living in Uganda. Al Jazeera reports that he was not critical of the government while in the military but grew increasingly opposed to President Paul Kagame. He ran a YouTube channel, "Major Robert TV", with 144,000 subscribers, and featured a song praising opposition figure Victoire Ingabire, who has been repeatedly imprisoned.

His brother, Victor Agaba, told the AFP news agency that Kabera had no issues with anyone in Uganda. "Our problem comes from home," he said, adding that the army created a criminal case against him that he called a witch-hunt. Al Jazeera reports that Kabera was declared a fugitive after leaving Rwanda and accused of corrupting a minor, charges he denied. The article does not report a response from Rwandan authorities to Agaba's comments, and police have not named a suspect or motive.

Al Jazeera notes that Rwandan authorities have been accused of assassinating opponents of Kagame, who has governed since coming to power in 2000. It lists earlier killings of exiled critics: Revocat Karemangingo, shot in Mozambique in 2021; Seif Bamporiki, shot in South Africa in 2021; and Patrick Karegeya, strangled in South Africa in 2014. Former general Faustin Kayumba Nyamwasa, who co-founded the Rwanda National Congress, has survived several attempts. The case remains under investigation.

Families in southern Somalia say relatives were killed or badly hurt during a November 2025 offensive around Jamaame that involved US air strikes and Somali ground forces, according to Al Jazeera. The outlet reports that US air operations against armed groups in Somalia have intensified sharply under President Donald Trump. US Africa Command (AFRICOM) records list 84 strikes through September 2026, while the New America Foundation counted 88.

One survivor, Maryam Haji Abdi Guled, said a munition struck near her home and wounded three of her six children. Her son Abdiqadir Salah, then seven, still has a metal fragment near his hip, and doctors have warned that removing it could leave him paralysed. She believes US drones carried out the attack. It took her more than 24 hours to reach medical care in Mogadishu. A Bimaal clan chief told Al Jazeera that many injured people remain in the town without access to such care.

AFRICOM acknowledged air strikes in the area on November 14 and 15, 2025, but disputes that its aircraft caused civilian casualties. It said its assessment of reports of 10 to 12 civilian deaths did not meet its "more likely than not" threshold. Al Jazeera notes that this does not establish that the strikes caused no harm. AFRICOM did not say whether investigators spoke to survivors, relatives or hospital staff, and said the review could be reopened with new information. It declined to disclose how many strikes were conducted, citing operational security.

Jubaland authorities said Somali and regional forces, including the US-trained Danab unit, killed at least 56 al-Shabab fighters and captured 20; Al Jazeera could not verify this. A UNHCR-led monitoring network documented 12 civilian deaths around Jamaame between November 16 and 18, 2025. Al Jazeera says the mix of air and ground fighting makes it hard to attribute individual deaths, and some witnesses declined to speak on the record, fearing reprisals.

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at an event in Manhattan on Monday night that the federal government has abdicated its role on artificial intelligence and that New Yorkers should resist the idea that the technology's spread cannot be stopped, according to TechCrunch.

He spoke at Webster Hall at The People's AI Assembly, hosted by the AI Now Institute, a think tank that studies the social implications of AI. Activist and "Broad City" star Ilana Glazer put questions to him. Mamdani argued that the rapid rollout is not inevitable and that public officials should hold AI companies accountable. "Nothing has to be," he said.

Mamdani pointed to steps his administration has taken. Last month he ordered a ban on AI use in elementary and middle schools, and over the summer he introduced a policy that would require landlords, brokers and real estate platforms to disclose when listing photos or videos are made with AI. Glazer, a parent, said AI in classrooms makes her nervous.

He criticized what he called a "complete abdication of federal law" and said national debate is often framed as an arms race with China, pushing humanistic concerns aside. He cited a February U.S. military strike on a school in Iran that killed more than 150 people. TechCrunch reported that officials involved in the Pentagon's internal investigation told Bloomberg that overreliance on AI in targeting was one factor.

TechCrunch said President Donald Trump's Superintelligence Task Force, announced earlier this month, largely focuses on allowing AI companies to self-regulate rather than creating new federal restrictions. A response from the administration was not included in the report. Mamdani said that after this federal administration, a very different framework for thinking about AI and accountability is needed.

Doctors at Mass General Brigham, a nonprofit academic healthcare system in Massachusetts, have built an AI tool that can estimate a person's biological age and predict a cancer patient's survival chances from a single photograph of the face, according to The Guardian. The study was published in the journal Lancet Digital Health.

The system was trained on more than 40 million facial photographs across a range of ethnicities and ages. It produced two tools. FAHR-FaceAge estimates biological age, meaning the age a person looks rather than their chronological age, and predicts cancer survival. FAHR-FaceSurvival predicts survival directly from the photo. The two were derived from the same model but captured different, complementary information and relied on different parts of the face.

Among US cancer patients treated with radiotherapy, those whom FAHR-FaceAge rated as looking five or more years older than their actual age had a 21 percent higher risk of dying during an average four-year follow-up. Those who looked five or more years younger had a 17 percent lower risk. Co-senior author Hugo Aerts said it was the first demonstration that an AI model can directly predict cancer survival from a simple photograph.

Radiation oncologist Dr Raymond Mak said the aim is to support personalised treatment decisions rather than replace physician judgment, by helping estimate frailty before intensive treatments. Researchers also found that heavy alcohol use, drug use and smoking were linked to looking biologically older, and that FAHR-FaceAge held up across variations in pose, lighting, expression and makeup.
Doctors cautioned that more research is needed before the tool could be widely used.

Pennsylvania's health department issued a health alert on Monday as cases of measles in pregnancy, and in turn congenital measles, continue to increase, according to Ars Technica. The department noted that congenital measles had not been seen in decades before the current outbreak. The alert includes clinical guidance for managing exposures and cases in pregnancy and in newborns.

As of October 19, Pennsylvania had reported 1,286 measles cases this year across 42 counties. Of those, 247 people were hospitalized and six reportedly died, though the latest death is still under state investigation. Ars Technica said reporting from The 19th earlier this month put measles cases during pregnancy at 53. The first death in the outbreak was a newborn boy who died right after birth while his mother was severely ill. The health department did not immediately respond to Ars Technica's request for information.

Ars Technica reported that measles in pregnancy raises the risk of hospitalization, pneumonia, ventilation, death, miscarriage, stillbirth, low birth weight and preterm labor. The MMR vaccine is not recommended during pregnancy because it is a live attenuated vaccine. Exposed pregnant people are advised to receive intravenous immunoglobulin, but only within six days of exposure.

Congenital cases vary widely, from no symptoms to severe multisystem disease and death. Symptoms can include fever, jaundice, low platelet counts, pneumonia and neurologic complications, and a rash may be delayed or atypical. Survivors face risks including immune amnesia and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, a progressive, fatal neurological disorder that can appear years later.

The alert says affected babies need long-term follow-up, and that parents should be counseled on early signs of that disorder, including seizures, regression in milestones and academic difficulties in older children.

Italy will send 500 army troops to "defend Milan" after two days of unrest in which demonstrators clashed with police, looted shops and vandalized property, Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini said on Monday, according to The Guardian. The deployment is expected to be part of a security package that the cabinet is due to approve on Tuesday.

Shops in central Milan closed early and boarded up windows, fearing more violence. Most stores on Via Montenapoleone, a luxury shopping street, removed merchandise from their windows while police patrolled. Several hundred hooded protesters, many believed to be minors, set bins on fire and looted stores in the city centre over the weekend after an initially peaceful Saturday demonstration over poor public services and rising costs. Decathlon, Arc'teryx and Vodafone shops were among those ransacked, according to television footage.

Police said they detained 271 young people in Milan on Sunday. Of those taken to police stations, 32 were arrested, including 23 minors and 13 foreign nationals, and 28 more were reported to judicial authorities. On Saturday, clashes also took place in Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo and Turin, where 28 protesters were arrested, according to a police report.

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who faces a national election next year, condemned the violence and chaired a meeting with ministers and security chiefs. Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said the government would respond firmly, including with measures to curb violence by minors. Corriere della Sera reported that Meloni was considering extending preventive detention for minors, cracking down on youth gangs and bringing forward parts of a security bill now before parliament.
The unrest echoed protests in France, where hundreds of thousands of people angered by living costs and declining public services marched on Saturday.

Protesters in Albania fought with riot police for a seventh consecutive day on Monday, the BBC reported. Many of the demonstrators are high school and university students seeking to oust Prime Minister Edi Rama. Official figures said 295 people had been injured before Monday's violence, 186 of them police officers.

A police station and government buildings in Tirana have been attacked. The protests are driven by demands for better university conditions, anger over corruption and calls for Rama's resignation. Holding up a rock thrown at police on Sunday, Rama told police chiefs that "the moment the state negotiates with this, the state has fallen." He said the protesters included young people "radicalised by dark forces in Europe and the US" and that Albania was the target of a "well co-ordinated attack." The BBC did not report evidence for that claim.

A BBC reporter in Rinia Park saw protesters prising up cobblestones before police advanced with a water cannon truck and tear gas. He also saw a policeman spray pepper spray in a young man's face at close range. Human rights lawyer Gentian Sejrani, who supports more than 100 arrested people, said police actions were often chaotic, that officers rarely present evidence in court, and that those throwing objects rarely get caught.

Activist Sidorela Vatnikaj, 27, a master's student in a movement without leaders, said she is uncomfortable with violence against authorities but blames police for starting it. She called for a technocratic government for one year to prepare democratic elections and accused Rama of rigging past elections and of ties to rich foreign investors and organized crime groups. The BBC did not report a response from Rama to those accusations.
Rama has been in power for 13 years and has promised EU membership by 2030, saying he is the only one who can deliver it.

Four people have died as torrential rain from Storm Adam brought severe flooding to eastern Spain, with evacuations and shelter-in-place orders affecting tens of thousands of people, authorities said on Monday, according to Al Jazeera. The storm began on Saturday and dropped as much as 700 litres of rain per square metre in 24 hours in parts of the Valencia region.

Two of the deaths occurred in the coastal resort of Oliva, a third at a beach in Sagunto, and a fourth involved a person who fell into a swollen stream in Catalonia. The storm also hit the Balearic Islands. Floodwaters isolated several towns on the Mediterranean coast, rivers burst their banks and streets turned into torrents. Al Jazeera said the scenes recalled the flooding two years ago that killed more than 230 people in the Valencia region.

On Monday morning, 800,000 residents were under shelter-in-place orders. By late afternoon that was reduced to 87,000 people in eight municipalities. About 100 municipalities had been told to stay indoors for several hours, and most restrictions were lifted by early afternoon as conditions improved, the regional government said. Government representative Pilar Bernabe said security forces carried out more than 400 rescues in the Valencia region, and people stranded on rooftops were winched to safety. The Civil Guard said more than 2,000 people were evacuated, mainly in Oliva.

In Els Poblets, cars and vans were piled on top of one another as residents tried to salvage belongings. Pego's mayor, Enrique Moll, said several people were still awaiting helicopter evacuation from rooftops and all access routes were blocked. Oliva's deputy mayor, Salvador Llopis, said emergency services were rescuing elderly residents trapped by waist-deep water.
Spain's weather agency AEMET said last month was mainland Spain's hottest September on record.

Iran's Foreign Ministry summoned Germany's ambassador, Axel Dittmann, after a Hamburg court convicted two men of plotting to kill two leaders of Jewish organisations at Tehran's behest, Al Jazeera reported. Iran accused Berlin of making "baseless political allegations." The move followed Germany's Monday summoning of Iranian ambassador Majid Nili Ahmadabadi over the alleged plot.

The court convicted a Danish national and an Afghan national on Thursday of planning to target Josef Schuster, president of Germany's main group representing the Jewish community, and Volker Beck, head of the German-Israeli society. The Dane, partially identified as Ali Hassan S, was jailed for eight and a half years. The Afghan, recruited as his accomplice, received four and a half years. Both were arrested in Denmark last year and extradited.

The court said Iran's intelligence service steered the two men, and the judge described their actions as "terrorist activities orchestrated by Iran." The German Foreign Ministry said the assassination attempts would have legal consequences, that Germany does not tolerate attacks on Jewish life and those who defend it, and that Tehran would not be allowed to "threaten our free society."

In a statement carried by the state news agency IRNA, Iran's Foreign Ministry said accusing Iran of security-related offences has long been a tactic of Israel and certain Western nations. It said giving a "judicial face" to baseless claims lends them no credibility and undermines the standing of the German judiciary. When the two men were charged, the Iranian embassy in Berlin likewise rejected what it called unfounded allegations made at the behest of Iran's enemies.

Myanmar has delivered gifts from King Charles to detained former leader Aung San Suu Kyi and released rare photos of her, in what critics called a stunt by the military to end the country's diplomatic isolation, The Guardian reported. A presidential spokesperson said home ministry officials handed over two gardening books on soil, plus a sealed envelope and a sealed diplomatic pouch. The photos showed her smiling in a wood-panelled room.

Suu Kyi, 81, a Nobel Peace laureate, is serving multiple sentences under house arrest at an undisclosed location in Naypyidaw. She was deposed in a 2021 military coup, which triggered a civil war that the monitor ACLED says has killed more than 100,000 people. Her whereabouts and health were hard to determine until an International Committee of the Red Cross visit in August.

Coup leader Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president in April after elections widely condemned as a sham. He has since visited Laos, Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia and, this month, Malaysia, where he received an official welcome. Asean had barred him from its summits for not following its peace plan. He remains under US sanctions for human rights abuses, including the 2016-2017 killings and expulsions of Rohingya Muslims, which Washington considers genocide. Myanmar has denied the accusations. He has also sought cooperation with the Trump administration, and Reuters reported US and Myanmar officials held talks.

Her son, Kim Aris, welcomed the gifts but said the regime must not use "selective disclosures to create an illusion of normality or gain international legitimacy," adding that his mother's rights continue to be violated. Phil Robertson of the Asia Human Rights and Labour Advocates group called the episode part of Myanmar's "quest for global legitimacy." The government's response to the critics was not included in the report.

Australian independent MP Helen Haines lost a leg after being struck by a car outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, Victoria, on Monday, according to The Guardian and Al Jazeera. She was flown to the Alfred hospital in Melbourne for emergency surgery. The Guardian reported that surgeons were trying on Tuesday to save her other leg and that the 65-year-old remained in a critical condition.

A 43-year-old man from Tarrawingee was arrested at the scene. The Guardian said it had confirmed his name as Brendan Nugent. The Australian Federal Police said it was working with state police to identify potential charges, including causing harm to a Commonwealth public official, which carries a maximum of 10 years in prison. Police were expected to interview him on Tuesday.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said it was a deliberate act, not an accident, and that the motive was unknown. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke told ABC radio that witnesses said the driver made a U-turn, pinned Haines against a vehicle, then reversed and did it again. Barber Ricky Jefferies, who works next door, pulled the driver out and held him until police arrived. He alleged the driver had a knife that he threw away without pulling it out.

The federal police said the incident appeared isolated, with no known further threats. Burke said there were 1,067 reports of harassment or threats against high office holders in the last financial year, up from 951, and that agencies would examine what more could have been done. Albanese and other leaders called for calmer political debate.

Vice President JD Vance declined on Monday to endorse Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's reelection bid, saying he intends to stay out of Israel's election. Fox News, citing Politico, reported the remarks came in an interview with Mark Halperin on "2WAY Tonight."

Vance said his focus is on American candidates ahead of the midterms. "I endorse American candidates, and that's where I'm focused on in the midterms. So I'm not getting involved in Israeli elections," he said. He added that his position should not be read as opposition to Netanyahu: "I'm not anti-endorsing him. I'm not pro-endorsing him."

The comments came a day after President Donald Trump gave Netanyahu what he called his "Complete and Total Endorsement" in a Truth Social post. Trump praised Netanyahu as a "Great Warrior Prime Minister" and a partner in confronting Iran, and wrote that Netanyahu "will never let you down." Netanyahu thanked Trump for what he called an "extraordinary endorsement" and said Israel has never had a greater friend in the White House.

Fox News noted that Vance has weighed in on a foreign contest before. According to Politico, he traveled to Hungary in April and campaigned alongside then-Prime Minister Viktor Orban shortly before Orban lost his reelection bid. Fox News said the White House could not immediately be reached for comment on Vance's latest remarks.

The Justice Department said on Monday it was charging 28 noncitizens in California with election crimes, and it filed an emergency federal court request to stop the state from processing ballots returned by voters it calls "likely noncitizens," NPR reported. The state has asked how the federal government reached its conclusions but has not received that information, according to NPR.

DOJ officials said all 28 defendants are green-card holders who appeared on a list of 20,000 names given to California officials last week. NPR reported that some do not appear to have voted and some registered more than 20 years ago. Many are accused of making false statements on naturalization applications. First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said that registering is "not something that just happens to you." Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said the department "will not look the other way" on noncitizen voting.

The dispute has escalated. Local and state officials declined to investigate the 20,000 names within a 48-hour deadline, and the federal government sued. McCotter then warned in a letter that officials could face criminal prosecution for knowingly processing ballots cast by people federal agencies identify as noncitizens.

UCLA election law expert Rick Hasen said 28 allegations is small against more than 20 million registered voters, and he warned of risks of disenfranchising eligible voters. NPR noted that noncitizen voting has never been found to be widespread. Officials elsewhere, including Arizona's Pinal County recorder, told NPR they are watching closely.

A few months into President Donald Trump's second term, political appointees at the Department of Homeland Security asked the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, known as CISA, to secretly acquire a voting machine and hack it, according to a Defense One report. The report cited two former administration officials with knowledge of the request. The appointees wanted the findings passed to the White House.

One former official said career staffers were shocked. CISA normally works to stop hackers, and the agency was reportedly told not to alert the machine's vendor to any flaws, contrary to standard practice. The official said the request made staff fear they were being asked to take part in political interference. CISA employees told the appointees it was impossible, partly because the agents able to do it had been laid off by the Department of Government Efficiency. The appointees eventually stopped pressing, and the request was not acted on.

The report says the administration has laid off or pushed out more than 1,000 CISA employees, about one-third of the agency, and that the 2027 budget proposal would cut another $700 million. Several state election authorities said CISA gave them no help during key planning for the midterms. Arizona Secretary of State Adrian Fontes said the administration had "basically cut us off."

A White House spokesperson, Lauren Bis, declined an interview but said Trump has done more than any other president to ensure free and fair elections. DHS and CISA did not respond to the report's questions. Democratic lawmakers have called for an investigation into CISA's capacity.

Federal Judge Ana Reyes withdrew a request that the Justice Department refile a brief naming the career attorneys who signed it, after a Trump administration lawyer called the order "untenable," according to the Washington Examiner. She reversed course on Monday after a hearing over the planned overhaul of East Potomac Golf Links in Washington, D.C., ran past six hours. She said she had spoken with her clerks and thought it over.

NPR reported the hearing was tense. Days earlier Reyes had temporarily blocked the project. She pressed government lawyers, who had told the court the plan was only conceptual, about Trump's Sunday posts describing a final design. "Do I believe the president of the United States or do I believe you?" she asked. A Justice Department filing the day before said the plan was not final because the Park Service had not finished its review.

The case began in February, when a D.C. preservation group and two individuals sued, arguing a single championship-style course would raise costs for a facility meant to be open to all. In May the judge ordered notice of major construction. NPR said the government then notified the court it would remove up to 529 trees, and bulldozers began the next day. Reyes ordered a 24-hour halt and said she was "beyond disappointed."

The White House asked Reyes to step aside, accusing her of bias, and she declined. Trump wrote that she was a "crazed lunatic" and that work needed no court approval. The White House says it is following a 2019 preservation plan; plaintiffs say Trump's plans go beyond it.

Lawyers for Mahmoud Khalil, the former Columbia University graduate student and pro-Palestinian activist, filed an emergency application with the Supreme Court on Monday, according to Al Jazeera. They are seeking an immediate stay of a ruling by the 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals in Philadelphia, and the Washington Examiner reported they have also asked the justices to take up the case.

The 3rd Circuit found that federal law should have barred lower courts from ordering Khalil's release from immigration detention in June 2025. It said his detention should first have been weighed in immigration court, which the executive branch oversees, rather than in federal district court. The question put to the justices is whether he can challenge his detention in federal court before the immigration proceedings end.

Khalil, a permanent U.S. resident, was arrested in March 2025 and held for more than three months. Al Jazeera reported he faces deportation to Algeria or Syria if the ruling holds. In May the 3rd Circuit voted six to five against reconsidering the case, but its decision does not take effect until his appeals are exhausted. In April the Board of Immigration Appeals denied his appeal and issued a final removal order, and his habeas corpus case remains ongoing.

His lawyers want the court to rule that noncitizens can sue if detained in retaliation for protected speech. Khalil said that if the administration can punish pro-Palestine speech, a future one can punish anyone. The administration has said it has the legal right to deport noncitizens who join such protests, characterizing the activism as a threat to U.S. foreign policy interests.

The Department of Homeland Security said more than 100,000 Ukrainians and Sudanese in the United States retain protection from deportation, after their temporary protected status was set to expire Monday, The Guardian reported. About 101,000 Ukrainians and 1,800 Sudanese were affected. DHS said an announcement "will be made at the appropriate time." It did not say how long the protection would last or when a final decision would come, and it did not answer whether work permits would continue. TPS generally allows people to work while protections remain.

The Guardian said the move follows a similar one about a month ago, when the administration kept protections in place for nearly 200,000 Salvadorans whose status was due to expire on Sept. 9. The administration has terminated TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria.

Reactions differed. Yuriy Boyechko of the nonprofit Hope For Ukraine called the step a "bandage" and urged a path to permanent residency, saying people cannot safely return to Ukraine. Andrew Arthur of the Center for Immigration Studies, which favors lower immigration, said the government faces no deadline and called it "simply going to be an extension until it is a termination." He said ongoing armed conflict in both countries gives the secretary authority to continue TPS.

Ukraine was designated for TPS in April 2022, and the Biden administration extended it in January 2025 through October 2026. Sudan's program dates to 1997. The decision comes two weeks before the midterm elections.
Ahead of the midterms, President Donald Trump has claimed he has boosted incomes, reduced inflation and created jobs. BBC Verify checked those claims against the data and found a mixed picture.

On growth, the economy is expanding at an annualized 2.2% and has grown about 3.2% since the end of 2024, more than any other G7 member, the BBC reported. It said the economy has been helped by an AI investment boom and could falter if that spending dried up.

Inflation is 3.7%, well below the 9% peak in 2022 under Joe Biden but above the 3% Trump inherited. The BBC said economists estimate tariffs pushed prices up, and the war with Iran raised energy costs. Diesel hit a record $6.52 a gallon in September. Beef and coffee prices have risen, while eggs have fallen.

Median household income, adjusted for inflation, rose 2.6% in 2025 to a record $87,460. But the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy estimates that tax cuts, expired health insurance subsidies and price rises leave the middle fifth of households about $1,700 worse off in 2026 than otherwise, and the richest 1% about $12,560 better off.

Job growth has averaged 34,000 a month in Trump's second term, versus 122,000 a month in Biden's final year, and manufacturing employment is slightly lower. Unemployment is 4.2%, roughly unchanged, which the BBC partly attributes to immigration enforcement shrinking the workforce.
The federal deficit was $2 trillion in the year to September, around 6% of GDP, and is projected to exceed 8% by 2030.

Nvidia said it plans to invest in four German startups, part of a commitment of nearly $10 billion to back companies, universities and research institutions across Europe, CNBC reported. The announcement came on Monday at the Invest in Germany Summit in Berlin. Nvidia did not disclose the size of the planned investments.

The startups are Agile Robots, which makes AI-powered robots for manufacturing, logistics and healthcare; Avelios Medical, which builds hospital management software; Mirelo, which develops AI models that generate audio for video; and Reflex Aerospace, which designs and builds satellites.

At the same event, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Germany aims to lead in bringing AI into key sectors, naming manufacturing, machinery and automobiles. He urged small and medium-sized businesses to use the data they already hold. "Please open your doors for AI to make use of your data," he said. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said AI "can only augment your capability, it will not replace your capability."

Nvidia is also expanding its work with the German government and the Industry 4.0 Platform, which brings together government, industry, research and trade groups. The government signed a joint declaration of intent with Nvidia on advancing AI models for industrial use. Earlier Monday, Siemens announced AI tools developed with Nvidia at its Erlangen factory, saying they could cut production-preparation engineering work by up to 85% and production-planning costs by as much as 20%.
Huang visited France last week to announce investments in four French startups. He is scheduled to give a keynote in Berlin on Wednesday.
